author: blu
body: The kernel capability bits live in Foreword chapter Capability. They were written out here as kern-cap-* and again in the compiler as cap-*, identical in all 23 names and all 23 values, and a binary is granted its authority by ONE of those two paths and must not get a different answer depending on which. Two were once missing here, and their absence WAS the disagreement: the boot path set cap-console (bit 0) and granted a Concurrent program ipc + process-create, and the loader granted neither, so the SAME binary could spawn a process when booted and could not when loaded. One table now, cited by both quires.

author: blu
body: A grant is a set of bits AND the extent over which they hold. The bitmask alone was the whole grant here, and the scope the verifier had already decoded was thrown away one line later -- so a binary whose manifest said "filesystem read, under /config/" was loaded with filesystem read over the ENTIRE volume. The authority survived the journey and the limit on it did not, which is the worst half to lose.

author: blu
body: Only the filesystem scope is carried, because it is the only one with a runtime chokepoint to enforce it (Fat16). A network authority and a console channel are checked at compile time and nowhere else, and a grant record that carried them would be claiming an enforcement that does not exist.

author: blu
body: The filesystem grant's scope, which the loader writes into the process table beside the bits. An absent filesystem capability and a filesystem capability with no scope both answer "" -- the empty prefix, which admits every path. That is the honest reading of an unscoped grant and it is what Fat16 already does with an empty scope, so the two agree by construction rather than by coincidence.

author: blu
body: The network authority scope, decoded the same way as the filesystem path scope but off the network capability. A loaded binary that declared [Network.Write "api.example.com"] carries that authority in its manifest; apply-load-decision installs it into the process's network scope cell so the fetch chokepoint enforces it at runtime.

author: blu
body: A DENIED load has no scope, and answering "" for it is not a hole: a denied decision writes nothing into the process table at all, so the empty string here is never installed anywhere. apply-load-decision is what enforces that, and it refuses before it writes either half.
